_about: Every number and quote the game shows, with where it came from. Net worths move by billions a day; the game rounds and says so. Lego set = $20 (the boys' unit). One money bag = $434 million (21.7 million Lego sets), chosen so Trump's fortune is exactly 15 bags, the number the market needs. Each quote carries a kid_text: our simpler words for a 5- and 7-year-old, shown as 'in kid words' with his exact words underneath. Each boss carries net_worth_as_of: the figures come from different dates (Trump's from March 2026, the others from September and October), so the game shows the date. gain.usd_per_day is how fast a heap grows in the game; it is 0 for a boss whose fortune shrank over the year. The four bosses added 10/31 (Zuckerberg, Page, Walton, Bloomberg) all use the Forbes 400 2026 figure (wealth as of September 4, 2026), and each carries a story object: the one thing he did, in kid words, with its source. Round 3 (10/31): a boss may carry display_name, the name shown and said in play (only walton: 'Rob Walton and family'); on-screen names use display_name || name. Every gate_true item and quote whose words hold a number above ten (a dollar figure, a year, million/billion) also carries play_text and play_why: the same fact with no number, for the voice and the screen in play (the number rule in docs/LESSON-PLAN.md). The original text and why stay as the grown-ups' record on the sources page.

gain.line: From March to September 2026, his pile grew by about $369 million every day. That is 18 million Lego sets a day.

source.title: Forbes World's Billionaires 2026 (Scripps News) and the Forbes 400 2026 (Forbes Australia)
source.note: Two Forbes figures, same method: Scripps list entry "1. Elon Musk — $839B (Tesla SpaceX)" (World's Billionaires list, share prices as of March 1, 2026) and Forbes 400: "Musk is now worth an estimated $908 billion" (Forbes 400, 'Forbes calculated net worths using share prices from September 4, 2026.'). Arithmetic: ($908B - $839B) / 187 days (2026-03-01 to 2026-09-04) = $368,983,957 a day = 18,449,198 Lego sets a day = 0.85 money bags a day. Over the full year Forbes 400 to Forbes 400 he went from $428B to $908B ("Elon Musk was already the richest American of all-time last year, with a fortune of $428 billion.").

taxes._about: The jar is the game's word for taxes. These are the sourced facts behind the prologue's 'this part is true' line and the jar card in the town square.
taxes.kid_text: Everybody puts a little in the jar. The jar pays for the school, the road and the fountain. That is what taxes are.

market._about: The Gerbil Market stands for the stock market and the whole economy. It got bigger; most of the new money went to the people who already had the most. Wealth groups are households ranked by wealth (Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts). The DFA cannot single out billionaires, so these items say 'richest' and give the group size.
market.kid_text: The market got bigger and bigger. But most of the new money went to the richest people.

items.line: Out of every $10 of stock that families own, the richest 1 family in 10 owns about $9. The poorer half of all families own 6 cents.
items.spoken: Out of every ten dollars of stock that families own, the richest one family in ten owns about nine dollars. The poorer half of all families own six cents.

source.title: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts: distribution of household wealth by wealth percentile, 2026:Q2 (released September 2026)
source.note: 2026:Q2 table, column 'Corporate equities and mutual fund shares': TopPt1 25.0, RemainingTop1 25.9, Next9 37.2, Next40 11.4, Bottom50 0.6 (percent). Top 1% = 25.0 + 25.9 = 50.9% (≈ $5 of $10); top 10% = 88.1%; bottom 50% = 0.6% (6 cents of $10). The Fed's definition excludes stock held inside 401(k)-type plans: 'Holdings of corporate equities and mutual fund shares excluding equities and mutual fund shares owned through DC pensions'. Read from the Fed's full CSV (dfa-networth-shares.csv).

items.line: From 2017 to 2025: if the stock market was 10 coins, it became 19. A family's pay went from 10 coins to 11.
items.spoken: From 2017 to 2025: if the stock market was ten coins, it became nineteen. A family's pay went from ten coins to eleven.

source.title: S&P 500 annual average (FRED series SP500), CPI-U (BLS, FRED series CPIAUCSL), real median household income (Census, FRED series MEHOINUSA672N)
source.note: Both after prices. S&P 500 annual average: 2017 2449.08, 2025 6216.87 (x2.538). CPI-U annual average: 2017 245.121, 2025 321.962, so in 2025 dollars the market grew 2.538 x 245.121 / 321.962 = 1.933, +93% (about $9 per $10). Real median household income (2025 dollars, Census, released 2026-09-15): 2017 $78,600, 2025 $87,460: +11.3% (about $1 per $10). Census 2026-09-15: 'Real median household income in 2025 was $87,460', a record. The S&P figure is the price index without dividends, so the true stock gain is larger. 2017 is the earliest year of FRED's ten-year S&P 500 series; that is why the span starts there. In coins (10 at the start): market 10 x 1.933 = 19.3, pay 10 x 87,460 / 78,600 = 11.1; rounded to 19 and 11.

items.line: Out of every $10 that families own, the richest 1 family in 10 has about $7. The poorer half of all families, together, have 23 cents.
items.spoken: Out of every ten dollars that families own, the richest one family in ten has about seven dollars. The poorer half of all families, all together, have twenty-three cents.

source.title: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts, 2026:Q2 (released September 2026)
source.note: 2026:Q2 table, column 'Net worth' share: TopPt1 15.0, RemainingTop1 17.5, Next9 36.4, Next40 28.8, Bottom50 2.3 (percent). Top 1% = 15.0 + 17.5 = 32.5% (about $3 of $10); bottom 50% = 2.3% (23 cents of $10). In 1989:Q3, the first quarter in the series, the top 1% had 22.8% and the bottom 50% had 3.5%. Top 10% = 15.0 + 17.5 + 36.4 = 68.9% (about $7 of $10).

items.line: Since 2015 families got $102 trillion of new money. For every $10 of it, the richest 1 family in 10 got $7. The poorer half of all families got 33 cents.
items.spoken: Since 2015, families got one hundred and two trillion dollars of new money. For every ten dollars of it, the richest one family in ten got seven dollars. The poorer half of all families got thirty-three cents.

source.title: Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts, net worth levels 2015:Q2 and 2026:Q2
source.note: Net worth levels, millions of dollars (dfa-networth-levels.csv). Total household net worth rose $102.46 trillion from 2015:Q2 to 2026:Q2. Top 10% (TopPt1 + RemainingTop1 + Next9) rose $69.77T = 68.1% of the increase (about $7 of $10); top 1% alone $34.88T = 34.0%; bottom 50% rose $3.36T = 3.3% (33 cents of $10). Not inflation-adjusted; the shares are the same either way.
